o: We may permute t arbitrarily while s stays fixed, maximizing the numeric value of s XOR t'. Work bit by bit from the most significant position: at each position, if s has a 1 we want a 0 from t (XOR gives 1); if s has a 0 we want a 1 from t. Each position consumes exactly one character of t, and the choices at different positions never conflict beyond consuming supply, so a greedy allocation is optimal. Example 3: s = 0101, t has two 1s and two 0s; placing 1s under s's zeros and 0s under s's ones yields 1111. With n up to 2e5 this greedy is O(n).
k: Greedy from the most significant bit: put t's 1s where s has 0s, and t's 0s where s has 1s, as long as supply lasts.
When supply runs out, the remaining positions are forced; the greedy is optimal because higher bits dominate the value.

a.i: Count zeros and ones in t. Scan s from left (most significant) to right: if s[i] = '1', spend a '0' from t if available (result bit 1), else spend a '1' (result bit 0); if s[i] = '0', spend a '1' if available (result bit 1), else spend a '0' (result bit 0). Higher bits always take priority, which is exactly the greedy exchange argument.
s: Count z = zeros in t, o = ones in t.
For each character c of s: if c = '1', emit '0' if z > 0 (z--) else '1' (o--).
If c = '0', emit '1' if o > 0 (o--) else '0' (z--).
Join emitted bits into the answer string.
a.t: O(n) — one counting pass plus one placement pass.

a.n: Approach 2: Direct construction of the rearranged t
a.i: Instead of emitting result bits, build the optimal rearrangement t' explicitly: place t's 1s at positions where s has 0 (as many as possible), then fill leftovers anywhere. XOR-ing s with t' produces the same maximum; useful if the problem later asks to output the rearrangement.
s: Count ones in t; reserve that many positions at indices where s = '0' (left to right).
Place remaining ones at unfilled positions left to right; fill the rest with zeros.
Return s XOR t' as a string.
a.t: O(n) — constant number of linear passes.
a.sp: O(n) for the constructed rearrangement and output.

w: Use the greedy bit-placement version; it is shorter and provably optimal by the dominance of high bits. Pitfall: when t runs out of the desired character, the bit is forced — do not forget to consume from the other bucket. Edge cases: all-zero t (answer equals s), all-one s with enough ones in t (answer all ones). Follow-up: maximize XOR under a limited number of rearrangement swaps, or minimize the XOR instead.
